Text:
My wife and I are a few years away from retirement, but we've spent a lot of time researching the possibility of eventually retiring in Malaysia.

One thing I've noticed is that there is no shortage of information about visas, property, healthcare and cost of living. All important topics of course.

What seems much harder to find are the lessons people only learn after they've actually made the move and lived here for a number of years.

The older I get, the more I realise there is rarely a perfect answer to anything. Most big decisions involve trade-offs, and I suspect retiring abroad is no different.

For those who have been living in Malaysia for five years or more, what do you know now that you wish you'd understood before you moved?

What did you gain that perhaps you hadn't expected?

What did you give up that you hadn't fully appreciated at the time?

If you could sit down with yourself six months before the move, what advice would you give?

I'd be genuinely interested to hear people's reflections.
F
author: Jasmine Tan

Text: My situation is slightly different to yours as I am a Brit, married to a Malaysian. I did a lot of research and made quite a few visits before deciding that I would be happy in Malaysia. That decision was made in 2010. We had a holiday home here from 2013 and retired here permanently in 2020. My only minor complaint is that it is almost impossible to get Permanent Residency here. On the plus side, the locals are friendly, the cost of living is much cheaper than in the UK (though the price of some imported items can make your eyes water a bit) and the food and climate are superb. I do have friends and family in the UK that I would like to see more of but the internet and all the social media apps mitigate that to a great extent. Whether you will be happy or not imho is not down to what Malaysia has to offer but is at least 70% down to coming with a positive attitude.

Text:
This is such a refreshing question. Most people get bogged down in the 'how-to' of visas and property, but you’re spot on—the real 'make or break' stuff usually comes down to the subtle trade-offs no one talks about until they’re actually here.

If I could pass on one piece of advice from my time here, it’s about 'social shorthand.' Back home, you have a rhythm—you know how things work, how to navigate the system, and how to relate to the people around you effortlessly. Here, you lose that shorthand for a while. You have to be comfortable being the 'student' again, even at this stage of your life. The biggest gain is the community and the pace of life, but the trade-off is that you have to be patient with a culture that operates on a different frequency than what you’re used to.

There are many so called foreign communities which i know mgs and so forth.

 Don't rush to plant roots. Rent in a few different areas for short stints first. Malaysia feels very different when you're a visitor versus when you're a resident, and your 'ideal' neighborhood might surprise you once you’re actually doing your weekly grocery runs there.

Also, from a practical standpoint— as I work in the local insurance space, I see a lot of expats who fall in love with the lifestyle but underestimate the 'longevity' side of things. Malaysia has fantastic private healthcare, but as a foreigner, medical inflation is also something that we may need to account for early. The best way to protect your retirement here is to have your 'staying power' (your health coverage) sorted out before you move, so that if health challenges arise than visas, well being of life  and property, you might can focus on enjoying your time in Malaysia rather than worrying about the lifestyle as malaysia is very welcome with a lot of foreign communities starting from kl expat and penang as well especially northern side straits quay as well

It’s an incredible place to retire, but it’s a marathon, not a sprint. Happy to chat more if you ever want a local perspective. Im a local chinese in penang.

Text:
Good morning,
My husband and I are in Malaysia under the MM2H silver program.

All papers are under his name and I am his dependent.

In case, God forbid, something happens to him, will I be able to stay with the MM2H program until the end of validity or will it be cancel automatically for dependants upon his death? 

Please advise  and wishing a great day to all members

No, your visa will not be automatically cancelled. Under the latest 2026 rules, the MM2H pass is transferable to the next-of-kin (spouse) in the event of the principal's passing. You will be allowed to stay until the end of the visa validity, and you can later apply to become the main applicant.

Text:
Florence Waller 
Under the Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) programme (Silver category):
If the principal applicant (your husband) passes away, the MM2H status is NOT automatically continued for dependants.
Your dependent pass is tied to his approval, so it may be cancelled.
However:
You can usually apply to transfer or convert the MM2H pass into your own name (becoming the principal applicant), subject to approval and meeting the requirements..

Text:
From what I understand under the current MM2H guidelines, the dependent’s pass is usually not cancelled immediately if something happens to the principal holder. In most cases, the spouse can continue to stay until the visa validity ends, and there may also be an option to apply to transfer or continue the pass, subject to approval by the authorities. It’s always good to double-check with your agent or Immigration for the exact procedure.

That said, many couples also look beyond the visa side and prepare financially for such unexpected situations. Having a dedicated savings plan in your own name can make things much smoother and provide financial security and independence if anything happens.

I personally work with FWD savings plans, which are quite popular among expatriates and MM2H families because they help build guaranteed savings over time while providing protection at the same time. Happy to share more information if it’s helpful.
